stated.text: The service is written in Node.js and uses no npm dependencies.
server.js listens on the port given in the PORT environment variable.
server.js keeps its data in the JSON file named by the DATA_FILE environment variable.
Groups and expenses survive a restart of the server (same DATA_FILE).
POST /groups with {"id": "<group id>", "members": ["<name>", ...]} creates a group and answers 201.
POST /groups answers 409 if a group with that id already exists.
POST /groups answers 400 unless members holds at least two distinct non-empty names.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses records an expense paid by one member (the payer).
An expense {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "equal"} is shared equally among all members of the group.
For split "equal", any cents left over after an even division go one each to the members listed first (in the group's members order).
An expense {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "exact", "shares": {"<name>": <cents>, ...}} makes each member listed in shares owe that many whole cents.
For split "exact", a share of zero is allowed.
For split "exact", the shares must add up to cents.
A recorded expense answers 201 with {"expense": <n>}, where n is 1 for the group's first expense, then 2, and so on.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown payer.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown member (a name in shares that is not a group member).
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for a non-positive amount.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for a non-integer amount.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown split.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for shares that do not add up to cents.
GET /groups/<id>/balances returns an object with each member's net cents: what they paid minus what they owe.
The balances returned by GET /groups/<id>/balances add up to 0.
GET /groups/<id>/settlements returns a JSON array of {"from", "to", "cents"} payments that bring every balance to 0.
Settlements are built by repeatedly having the member who owes most pay the member who is owed most the smaller of the two amounts.
In settlements, ties (between debtors or between creditors) go to the member listed first.
Every route under /groups/<id> answers 404 for an unknown group.
Concurrent requests must never lose an expense.
The behaviour is covered by node:test tests under test/ that run with `node --test`.

unstated.text: What happens to a request whose body is not valid JSON, or is missing fields, or has fields of the wrong type (id not a string or empty, members not an array, a member that is not a string, payer missing, cents as the string "100", shares not an object, split "exact" without shares).
unstated.why: Client code and the operator need a predictable error instead of a 500 or a crashed process; a crash would also take down every other group's service.
unstated.probe: Start the server. POST /groups with body `not json`; with {}; with {"id": 5, "members": ["a","b"]}; with {"id": "", "members": ["a","b"]}; with {"id": "g", "members": "a,b"}; with {"id": "g", "members": ["a", 7]}. Create group g with ["a","b"] and POST /groups/g/expenses with `not json`, with {"cents": 100, "split": "equal"}, with {"payer": "a", "cents": "100", "split": "equal"}, with {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "exact"}, with {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": [100]}. Record each status and body, then check the server still answers GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for each, with or without a JSON error message; any 4xx that is not a crash or 500 would also be acceptable. Treating a numeric string cents as invalid or coercing it are both defensible, but it should be consistent and not crash.

unstated.text: Whether exact shares may be negative or non-integer (for example {"a": -50, "b": 150} for cents 100, or {"a": 50.5, "b": 49.5}), since only the total is said to be checked.
unstated.why: A negative share lets someone record an expense that credits a member who paid nothing; fractional shares break the whole-cents balances and settlements the customer relies on.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["a","b"]. POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"a": -50, "b": 150}} and then {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"a": 50.5, "b": 49.5}}. Record the statuses and GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for both is the expected reading of 'whole cents (zero is allowed)'; accepting negative shares is a judgement call only if documented, fractional shares should not be accepted.

unstated.text: How duplicate names in members are handled when at least two distinct names remain (for example ["a", "a", "b"]), and whether names that differ only in case or surrounding spaces ("Ann", "ann", " Ann ") or that are whitespace only count as distinct non-empty names.
unstated.why: A duplicated member would be counted twice in an equal split and change who gets the leftover cents; customers typing names by hand will hit these cases.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "d", "members": ["a", "a", "b"]}; if 201, POST /groups/d/expenses {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "equal"} and GET /groups/d/balances. POST /groups {"id": "w", "members": [" ", "b"]} and {"id": "c", "members": ["Ann", "ann"]}; record statuses.
unstated.fine_answers: Rejecting duplicates with 400, or accepting and de-duplicating while keeping first-listed order, are both fine; a member must not be counted twice. Treating case variants as distinct is fine; whitespace-only names being rejected or accepted are both defensible if consistent.

unstated.text: Whether an exact split must list every member, i.e. what a member left out of shares owes.
unstated.why: Users splitting a bill among some of the group need to know whether omitted members are simply not charged or the request is refused.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["a","b","c"]. POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "a", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"b": 100}}; record the status and GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: Accepting with c owing 0 (the plain reading of 'each member listed in shares') is expected; requiring every member to be listed would contradict the request less clearly and should be documented if chosen.

unstated.text: Whether an acknowledged expense (201 returned) is already written to DATA_FILE, so a crash or kill right after the response does not lose it, and whether a crash during a write can leave DATA_FILE truncated or corrupt.
unstated.why: The customer was promised that expenses survive a restart and that none are lost; an operator restarting after a crash must not find an unreadable file and lose every group.
unstated.probe: Start the server with DATA_FILE=/tmp/x.json, create group g, POST an expense, and immediately send SIGKILL to the server process once the 201 arrives. Restart with the same DATA_FILE and GET /groups/g/balances; also check /tmp/x.json parses as JSON. Repeat while sending many POSTs in a loop and killing mid-stream; check the file still parses and every expense that got 201 is reflected.
unstated.fine_answers: Persist before replying and write atomically (temporary file then rename); a synchronous write before replying without atomic rename is weaker but may be acceptable for this scale.

unstated.text: What the server does at startup when DATA_FILE does not exist, is empty, or holds invalid JSON.
unstated.why: The operator's first start has no file; a corrupt file must not be silently overwritten with an empty store, which would wipe the customer's data.
unstated.probe: Start with DATA_FILE pointing to a path that does not exist and create a group; check the file is created. Stop, replace the file contents with `{broken`, start again; record whether it refuses to start, starts empty, or starts and later overwrites the file.
unstated.fine_answers: A missing file starts an empty store. For an empty or corrupt file, refusing to start with a clear error, or starting while preserving the bad file (e.g. renamed), are fine; silently overwriting it is not.

unstated.text: Whether concurrent expense posts to one group each get a distinct expense number with no duplicates or gaps, and concurrent creation of the same group id gives exactly one 201.
unstated.why: Expense numbers are how users refer to expenses; two expenses both numbered 3 or two 201s for one group would mean one was overwritten.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["a","b"]. Fire 100 POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "a", "cents": 1, "split": "equal"} at once; collect the returned numbers and check they are exactly 1..100, and GET balances shows a at +50, b at -50. Fire 20 concurrent POST /groups {"id": "race", "members": ["a","b"]}; count 201s and 409s. Restart and post one more expense; check it is numbered 101.
unstated.fine_answers: Exactly 1..N with no repeats, one 201 and the rest 409; numbering continues after restart.

unstated.text: How unknown paths and wrong methods are answered (GET /groups, DELETE /groups/g, POST /groups/g/balances, /groups/g/unknown, /other), and what Content-Type responses carry.
unstated.why: Client developers need to tell a typo from a missing group; the request only says unknown groups get 404.
unstated.probe: Create group g. Send GET /groups, DELETE /groups/g, POST /groups/g/balances, GET /groups/g/unknown and GET /other; record statuses and the Content-Type header of a normal 200 and of an error.
unstated.fine_answers: 404 or 405 for wrong method or path are both fine; JSON responses with Content-Type application/json are expected. The server must not hang or crash.

unstated.text: How group ids that are awkward in a URL are handled (ids containing '/', spaces, '%', or unicode), given ids arrive in the JSON body but are addressed in the path.
unstated.why: A group created with an id that cannot be addressed afterwards is effectively lost to the customer.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "a b", "members": ["x","y"]} and {"id": "a/b", "members": ["x","y"]}; for each 201, GET /groups/a%20b/balances and /groups/a%2Fb/balances and record whether they find the group.
unstated.fine_answers: Rejecting such ids with 400, or accepting them and decoding the path so they are reachable, are both fine; accepting an id that can never be reached is not.

unstated.text: What happens when PORT or DATA_FILE is not set.
unstated.why: An operator who forgets an environment variable should get a clear failure or a documented default, not data written to an unexpected place.
unstated.probe: Run `node server.js` with PORT unset and DATA_FILE set; then with DATA_FILE unset and PORT set. Record whether it exits with a message, uses a default, and where (if anywhere) it writes data.
unstated.fine_answers: Exit with a clear error, or use a documented default port and data file path; both fine.

unstated.text: Whether the tests are self-contained: they start their own server on a free port with a temporary DATA_FILE, need nothing already running, leave no stray files or processes, and pass when run repeatedly.
unstated.why: The next maintainer runs `node --test` on a fresh checkout or in CI; tests that need a fixed port or write into a real data file fail or clobber data.
unstated.probe: On a clean checkout with nothing listening, run `node --test` from the project root twice in a row, and once while another process holds a common port such as 3000; check the exit code is 0 each time, that no new files remain in the project folder, and that no node process is left running.
unstated.fine_answers: Any self-contained approach (spawning server.js on port 0 or a found free port, or importing the server) is fine.
